stem: A design review lists two separate gaps: attackers have been submitting SQL injection payloads through a public form, and the same application still stores its database password in a plaintext configuration file. Which TWO changes close these two specific gaps? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Attach an AWS WAF web ACL with a managed rule group for SQL injection
Subscribe to AWS Shield Standard for the public form's load balancer
Move the database password into AWS Secrets Manager with rotation turned on
Move the application's external customers into IAM Identity Center for sign-in
Bake the database password into the application's next AMI build

rationale: Attaching a WAF web ACL with a managed rule group written for SQL injection inspects and blocks the crafted requests before they reach the application, closing the first gap. Moving the database password into Secrets Manager with rotation turned on removes it from the plaintext configuration file and replaces it with a runtime retrieval, closing the second gap. Shield Standard is already enabled automatically for every account and defends against network- and transport-layer DDoS traffic; it does not inspect request content, so it does nothing against SQL injection payloads. IAM Identity Center federates workforce users into AWS accounts and permission sets; the application's external customers are not workforce users, so this does not apply here and does not touch either stated gap. Baking the password into the next AMI build still leaves it as a hard-coded credential in a build artifact, just relocated rather than removed.
